casimir_effect.goal: Two uncharged, perfectly conducting plates face each other across a narrow gap in empty space. Only vacuum modes whose half-wavelengths fit the gap survive between them. Sum the zero-point energy ½ħω of every allowed mode between the plates, subtract the same sum for free space, and write the energy per unit plate area as a function of the gap a.
casimir_effect.name: Casimir energy (Casimir, 1948)
casimir_effect.ask: After regularising (the divergent parts cancel), the result is −π²ħc/(720a³). Find its magnitude for the gap below, in units where ħc = 1.
casimir_effect.method: Each standing mode across the gap has kz = nπ/a; the energy is a sum over n and an integral over in-plane k. Subtract the continuum and regularise with ζ(−3) = 1/120.

quantum_entanglement.goal: Two photons are created in the joint polarisation state (|HH⟩ + |VV⟩)/√2. One passes a linear polariser at angle α, the other a polariser at angle β; a polariser at angle φ projects onto cos φ|H⟩ + sin φ|V⟩. Add the probabilities of both-pass and both-blocked (by symmetry they are equal) to write the probability that the two detectors agree.
quantum_entanglement.name: Bell-state polariser correlation (cos² rule)
quantum_entanglement.form: 2 * abs ( ( cos ( α ) * cos ( β ) + sin ( α ) * sin ( β ) ) / sqrt ( 2 ) ) ^ 2
quantum_entanglement.ask: The bracket is cos(α − β), so P = cos²(α − β). Find the probability that the detectors agree for the polariser angles below (in degrees).

vars.P: probability that both photons give the same result

quantum_entanglement.method: Project the pair state onto ⟨α|⊗⟨β|: the HH and VV parts give cos α cos β and sin α sin β, each with the 1/√2 of the state. Square the modulus and double it for the both-blocked outcome.

metamaterials.goal: A lattice of thin wires behaves like a dilute electron plasma for microwaves, and an array of split rings acts as tiny resonant LC circuits that respond to the magnetic field. Write the relative permittivity of the lossless wire plasma and the relative permeability of the ring array (a resonance at ω0 with filling factor F), and combine them into the refractive index, choosing the root that keeps energy flowing away from the source when both are negative.
metamaterials.name: Double-negative index of a Drude–Lorentz wire / split-ring medium
metamaterials.ask: Find the refractive index n (a negative number) at the frequency below.

vars.F: filling factor of the split rings

metamaterials.method: A free-electron plasma gives ε = 1 − ωp²/ω²; a driven resonator gives μ = 1 − Fω²/(ω² − ω0²). n² = εμ; when ε and μ are both negative the phase velocity is opposite to the energy flow, so take the negative root.

thermodynamics_of_information.goal: A one-bit memory holds 0 with probability p and 1 with probability 1 − p. Resetting it to a definite 0 removes its statistical entropy, which must be dumped as heat into surroundings at temperature T. Write the minimum work needed for the reset as a sum over the two states.
thermodynamics_of_information.name: Landauer's bound (Gibbs–Shannon entropy of a bit)
thermodynamics_of_information.form: - kB * T * sum ( j , 1 , 2 , p _ j * ln ( p _ j ) )
thermodynamics_of_information.ask: Find W/kB (in kelvin) for erasing a bit that reads 0 with probability p = 0.25, at T = 300 K.

vars.W: minimum work to reset the bit
vars.p: probability of a state (p_j); in the numeric step, probability of 0

thermodynamics_of_information.method: The entropy of a distribution is −kB Σ p ln p; after the reset it is zero. The second law demands at least T ΔS of heat into the surroundings, supplied as work.

genomics.goal: A genome of length G is shredded into N random reads of length L, each placed independently at a uniformly random position. A given base is covered by a read with probability L/G. Write the probability that a given base is covered by exactly k reads.
genomics.name: Lander–Waterman coverage statistics
genomics.form: binom ( N , k ) * ( L / G ) ^ k * ( 1 - L / G ) ^ ( N - k )
genomics.ask: For many reads this becomes a Poisson distribution of mean C = LN/G, so P₀ = e^(−C). Find the fraction of the genome covered at least once for L = 100 bp, N = 60 million reads and G = 3000 Mbp (L·N/G = 100 × 60 / 3000).

vars.k: number of reads covering the base

genomics.method: Each read is an independent trial that covers the base or not: count the ways to choose which k of the N reads cover it.

nanochemistry.goal: A nanotube is a strip of graphene rolled up so that the lattice vector n a⃗1 + m a⃗2 wraps exactly once around the circumference. The two lattice basis vectors of graphene have equal length and meet at 60°. Write the diameter of the tube using the dot product of the wrapping vector with itself.
nanochemistry.name: Carbon tube diameter from the chiral vector (n, m)
nanochemistry.form: sqrt ( ( n * vec ( a _ 1 ) + m * vec ( a _ 2 ) ) · ( n * vec ( a _ 1 ) + m * vec ( a _ 2 ) ) ) / π
nanochemistry.expr: a * sqrt ( n ^ 2 + n * m + m ^ 2 ) / π
nanochemistry.ask: With |a⃗1| = |a⃗2| = a and a⃗1·a⃗2 = a²/2 the diameter is a√(n² + nm + m²)/π. Find d (nm) for a (10,10) armchair tube with a = 0.246 nm.
nanochemistry.method: The circumference is the length of the wrapping vector; expand its square with the dot product of the two basis vectors. Diameter = circumference / π.

annihilation_power.goal: A particle and its antiparticle, each of rest mass m, meet with momenta p⃗1 and p⃗2 and annihilate completely into radiation. A reactor converts a fraction η of the radiation into useful energy. Write the useful energy as the sum of the two particles' total relativistic energies.
annihilation_power.name: Annihilation energy from the energy–momentum relation
annihilation_power.ask: In a trap both particles are essentially at rest. Find the useful energy in MJ when 1 μg (1e-9 kg) of antimatter annihilates with 1 μg of matter at efficiency η = 0.5.

vars.p: momentum (p₁ of the particle, p₂ of the antiparticle)

annihilation_power.method: Each particle's total energy follows from E² = p²c² + m²c⁴; all of it is converted to photons, so add both energies and apply the efficiency.

neutrino_physics.goal: A neutrino is born as a flavour state that is a rotation, by mixing angle θ, of two mass states with squared masses differing by Δm². Each mass state picks up a phase m²L/(2E) as it travels a distance L at energy E (natural units). Write the probability that it is detected as the other flavour.
neutrino_physics.name: Two-flavour neutrino oscillation probability
neutrino_physics.ask: In practical units the phase is 1.267 Δm²[eV²] L[km] / E[GeV]. Find P for θ = 0.6 rad, Δm² = 0.0025 eV², L = 250 km and E = 1 GeV.

vars.Δ: difference (Δm² is the difference of the squared masses)

neutrino_physics.method: Write the flavour state in the mass basis, evolve each component with its own phase, and project onto the other flavour. Only the phase difference survives in |amplitude|².

brane_cosmology.goal: Our universe is a 4D membrane at one end of a fifth dimension y running from −πr to πr, and the 5D metric shrinks the 4D part by a warp factor e^(−2k|y|). The 5D gravity strength M³ is turned into the 4D one by integrating the action over y: the volume element contributes e^(−4k|y|) and the 4D curvature term e^(+2k|y|). Write the effective 4D Planck mass squared.
brane_cosmology.name: Randall–Sundrum warped extra dimension (effective 4D gravity scale)
brane_cosmology.form: M ^ 3 * int ( - π * r , π * r , exp ( - 4 * k * abs ( y ) ) * exp ( 2 * k * abs ( y ) ) , y )
brane_cosmology.ask: The integral gives (M³/k)(1 − e^(−2kπr)) ≈ M³/k, so M and k are of order the Planck scale - yet a mass m0 on the far brane at |y| = πr appears to us reduced by the warp factor e^(−kπr). Find the apparent mass (GeV) of m0 = 1.22e19 GeV for k = 1 and r = 11.5 (in units of 1/k).

vars.m0: mass parameter on the hidden brane

brane_cosmology.method: Reduce the 5D action ∫d⁴x dy √−G M³ R over y: √−G carries four powers of the warp factor e^(−k|y|), the inverse metric in R removes two. Integrate the leftover exponential over both halves of the orbifold.

hyperdimensional_geometry.goal: In n dimensions a ball of radius r is a nest of thin spherical shells. The surface area of the unit sphere in n dimensions follows from evaluating the n-dimensional Gaussian integral in Cartesian and in spherical coordinates. Write the volume of the n-ball as an integral over shells of radius ρ.
hyperdimensional_geometry.name: Hypervolume of an n-ball (shell integral)
hyperdimensional_geometry.ask: The integral is π^(n/2) r^n / Γ(n/2 + 1). Find the 4-volume of a 4-ball of radius r = 2 (Γ(3) = 2).
hyperdimensional_geometry.method: (∫e^(−x²)dx)^n = π^(n/2) in Cartesian coordinates, and S_(n−1)∫ρ^(n−1)e^(−ρ²)dρ = S_(n−1)Γ(n/2)/2 in spherical ones; equate to get the sphere area, then integrate shells.

real_analysis.goal: Add a, then a·r, then a·r², and so on, stopping after the N-th power. The value of the infinite series is defined as what these partial sums approach as N grows without bound. Write that value.
real_analysis.name: Geometric series as a limit of partial sums
real_analysis.form: lim ( N , ∞ , sum ( k , 0 , N , a * r ^ k ) )
real_analysis.ask: For |r| < 1 the partial sum a(1 − r^(N+1))/(1 − r) converges. Find S for a = 3 and r = 0.4.
real_analysis.method: Multiply the partial sum by r and subtract it from itself to get a closed form, then let N → ∞.

stellar_evolution.goal: A star stays on the main sequence until it has burnt a fraction f of its mass M, and fusing hydrogen releases 0.7% of the burnt mass as energy. Its luminosity scales with mass to the power 3.5 relative to the Sun. Write its main-sequence lifetime as the burnt mass integrated against energy released per unit mass divided by luminosity.
stellar_evolution.name: Stellar lifetime from the mass–luminosity relation
stellar_evolution.ask: Find the lifetime in billions of years of a star of M = 2 solar masses with f = 0.1.

vars.M: stellar mass (in the numeric step: in solar masses)

stellar_evolution.method: Energy per burnt mass is 0.007c²; divide by the (constant) luminosity, which follows L ∝ M^3.5, and integrate over the burnt mass.

antiatom_chemistry.goal: An antiproton and a positron are bound by the same Coulomb attraction as a proton and an electron. Treat the two-body problem with the reduced mass of the pair, quantise the angular momentum, and write the energy of the n-th bound level in terms of the masses, the elementary charge, the vacuum permittivity and the Planck constant.
antiatom_chemistry.name: Bohr levels of (anti)hydrogen with reduced mass
antiatom_chemistry.ask: CPT symmetry makes antihydrogen's levels identical to hydrogen's: E_n = −R/n² with R = 13.606 eV. Find the photon energy (eV) of the 2 → 1 transition probed by laser spectroscopy.
antiatom_chemistry.method: Balance the Coulomb force against the centripetal force of the reduced mass, impose L = nħ, then add kinetic and potential energy.

component_tiers.goal: A structure is a chain of N parts and fails as soon as its weakest part fails. Part j carries stress σj; below a threshold stress σu nothing ever breaks, and above it the probability of surviving falls off as a stretched exponential with scale σ0 and modulus m. Write the survival probability of the whole structure.
component_tiers.name: Weakest-link (three-parameter Weibull) survival
component_tiers.form: prod ( j , 1 , N , exp ( - ( ( σ _ j - σ _ u ) / σ _ 0 ) ^ m ) )
component_tiers.ask: If every part carries the same stress the product becomes exp(−N((σ − σu)/σ0)^m). Find P for N = 10, σ = 0.5 σ0, σu = 0.1 σ0, m = 3.

vars.σ: stress (σ_j on part j, σ_u threshold, σ_0 scale)

component_tiers.method: The structure survives only if every part does, so multiply the independent part survival probabilities.

research_synthesis.goal: A machine gets faster with practice: every time its cumulative number of completed tasks doubles, the time per task is multiplied by the progress ratio r. The first task took T1. Write the total time to complete the first n tasks as a sum, with the exponent of the task number expressed through logarithms.
research_synthesis.name: Wright's learning curve (cumulative time)
research_synthesis.form: sum ( k , 1 , n , T _ 1 * k ^ ( log ( r ) / log ( 2 ) ) )
research_synthesis.ask: Approximate the sum by the integral ∫₀ⁿ T1 k^(−b) dk = T1 n^(1−b)/(1−b), with b = −log₂ r. Find the total time (hours) for n = 8 tasks, T1 = 100 h and r = 0.8.
research_synthesis.method: If each doubling multiplies the time by r, the k-th task takes T1·r^(log₂ k) = T1·k^(log₂ r). Add the tasks one by one.

dyson_sphere.goal: A thin closed shell of radius r surrounds a star and absorbs all of its light. In equilibrium the shell radiates the star's whole luminosity from its outer surface only, as a black body at uniform temperature T. Write that luminosity as the radiated flux integrated over the shell in spherical coordinates.
dyson_sphere.name: Radiative equilibrium of a closed shell (Stefan–Boltzmann)
dyson_sphere.form: int ( 0 , π , int ( 0 , 2 * π , σ * T ^ 4 * r ^ 2 * sin ( θ ) , φ ) , θ )
dyson_sphere.ask: The integral is 4πr²σT⁴. Find the equilibrium temperature (K) of a shell at r = 0.7 AU around a star of L = 0.5 solar luminosities.

vars.L: stellar luminosity (in the numeric step: in solar luminosities)
vars.σ: radiation constant of a black body
vars.r: shell radius (in the numeric step: in AU)

dyson_sphere.method: Each area element r² sin θ dθ dφ emits σT⁴; integrate over the full sphere and set the total equal to the luminosity, then solve for T.

holographic_principle.goal: The maximum entropy that fits inside a region is set not by its volume but by the area of its boundary: one quarter of a unit of kB for every Planck area (Għ/c³) of the enclosing surface. Write the entropy of a spherical horizon of radius r by integrating the area element over the sphere.
holographic_principle.name: Bekenstein–Hawking entropy (area law)
holographic_principle.form: kB * c ^ 3 / ( 4 * G * ħ ) * int ( 0 , π , int ( 0 , 2 * π , r ^ 2 * sin ( θ ) , φ ) , θ )
holographic_principle.ask: The integral gives S = πkB r²/l², with l the Planck length. Find the information capacity in bits (S/(kB ln 2)) of a horizon of radius r = 1000 Planck lengths.
holographic_principle.method: Integrate r² sin θ over the sphere to get the area, then divide by four Planck areas (4Għ/c³) and multiply by kB.

synthetic_biology.goal: A culture starts with N0 cells that divide every τ hours, but the vessel can only support K cells: growth slows in proportion to how full it is. Solve the growth equation with this crowding term and write the number of cells at time t, with the growth rate expressed through the doubling time.
synthetic_biology.name: Logistic growth (solution of the Verhulst equation)
synthetic_biology.expr: K * N0 * exp ( ln ( 2 ) * t / τ ) / ( K + N0 * ( exp ( ln ( 2 ) * t / τ ) - 1 ) )
synthetic_biology.ask: Find the number of cells after t = 24 h, starting from N0 = 1000 with τ = 2 h and capacity K = 1e9.

vars.N: number of cells (N₀ at the start)

synthetic_biology.method: The rate is dN/dt = (ln2/τ)·N(1 − N/K). Separate variables with partial fractions, integrate and solve for N.

morphogenesis.goal: An activator molecule a spreads by diffusion, catalyses its own production (in proportion to a² and inhibited by a second molecule h, with saturation κ at high a), decays at rate μ, and is also produced at a small basal rate. Write the rate of change of the activator concentration.
morphogenesis.name: Gierer–Meinhardt activator equation (Turing-type reaction–diffusion)
morphogenesis.ask: Far from the source, where production is negligible, the steady state obeys D∇²a = μa, solved by a = a0·e^(−x√(μ/D)). Find a/a0 at x = 50 µm for D = 10 µm²/s and μ = 0.001 /s.
morphogenesis.method: Add up the processes acting on a: diffusion (Laplacian), autocatalysis divided by inhibition and saturation, linear decay and a constant source.

quantum_field_theory.goal: A free scalar field is a collection of independent harmonic oscillators, one for every wave vector k. Each oscillator has a lowering operator that destroys a particle and a raising operator that creates one, multiplying a plane wave e^(∓ik·x) of the field's 4-momentum. Write the field operator as an integral over all momenta with the relativistically normalised measure.
quantum_field_theory.name: Mode expansion of the free Klein–Gordon field
quantum_field_theory.form: iiint ( ( hat ( a ) * exp ( - i * ( k · x ) ) + dag ( hat ( a ) ) * exp ( i * ( k · x ) ) ) / ( ( 2 * π ) ^ 3 * sqrt ( 2 * ω ) ) , k )
quantum_field_theory.ask: Each mode oscillates at the frequency fixed by the field equation, ω² = |k|² + m² (ħ = c = 1). Find ω for a particle of mass m = 0.6 with |k| = 0.8.

vars.a: annihilation operator of mode k (a† creates)
vars.k: 4-momentum of the mode (|k| in the numeric step)

quantum_field_theory.method: Solve the free field equation by Fourier transform; each k gives positive and negative frequency solutions whose coefficients become a and a†. Normalise with 1/√(2ω) so the measure is Lorentz invariant.

superconductivity.goal: Electrons near the Fermi surface attract each other through lattice vibrations, but only within the Debye energy ħωD of it, with dimensionless coupling λ. At the critical temperature the pairing gap just vanishes, and the self-consistency condition reduces to an integral over the electron energy ξ weighted by the thermal occupation factor. Write that condition.
superconductivity.name: BCS gap equation at the critical temperature
superconductivity.form: λ * int ( 0 , ħ * ω _ D , tanh ( ξ / ( 2 * kB * Tc ) ) / ξ , ξ )
superconductivity.ask: For weak coupling the integral gives kB Tc = 1.13 ħωD e^(−1/λ). Find Tc (K) for a hydride with Debye temperature Θ = ħωD/kB = 1800 K and λ = 0.5.

vars.ξ: electron energy from the Fermi level

superconductivity.method: Set the gap to zero in the self-consistent gap equation; the thermal factor 1 − 2f(ξ) becomes tanh(ξ/2kBT). For λ ≪ 1 the integral is ≈ ln(1.13ħωD/kBTc).

general_relativity.goal: The curvature of spacetime, built from the metric g_μν and its derivatives (Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar), must be sourced by the energy and momentum of matter, T_μν, with a coupling fixed so that weak fields reproduce Newtonian gravity; a constant vacuum energy may also contribute in proportion to the metric. Write the source side of the field equations.
general_relativity.name: Einstein field equations with cosmological constant
general_relativity.form: 8 * π * G / c ^ 4 * T _ μν - Λ * g _ μν
general_relativity.ask: The vacuum spherically symmetric solution has g_tt = −(1 − rs/r) with rs = 2GM/c². Find rs (m) for the Sun, M = 1.989e30 kg.
general_relativity.method: Require the field equation to be a rank-2 tensor equation whose divergence vanishes (energy conservation) and whose weak-field limit is ∇²Φ = 4πGρ; this fixes the 8πG/c⁴ coupling.

island_of_stability.goal: Treat a nucleus of Z protons and A nucleons as a charged liquid drop. Its binding energy gains a fixed amount per nucleon from the bulk, loses some from the surface (∝ A^(2/3)), from the mutual repulsion of the protons (∝ Z(Z−1)/A^(1/3)) and from any imbalance between neutrons and protons (∝ (A − 2Z)²/A), plus a small pairing correction. Write the binding energy.
island_of_stability.name: Semi-empirical mass formula (Bethe–Weizsäcker liquid drop)
island_of_stability.ask: Fission sets in when the Coulomb term outgrows twice the surface term; the fissility is x = (aC Z²/A^(1/3)) / (2 aS A^(2/3)). Find x for flerovium-298 (Z = 114, A = 298) with aS = 17.8 MeV and aC = 0.711 MeV.

vars.a: coefficient (a_V volume, a_S surface, a_C Coulomb, a_A asymmetry)

island_of_stability.method: Volume energy ∝ A; the surface ∝ R² ∝ A^(2/3); Coulomb energy of a uniformly charged sphere ∝ Z(Z−1)/R; the Pauli principle penalises N ≠ Z quadratically.

matrioshka_brain.goal: A star of luminosity L is enclosed by computing shells; the outermost, of radius R, radiates everything to space as a black body. Every erased bit must leave as entropy, at kB ln 2 per bit, and black-body radiation of power L at temperature T carries entropy 4L/(3T) per second. Write the maximum rate of bit erasures, with the shell temperature fixed by radiative balance.
matrioshka_brain.name: Landauer-limited computation of a stellar shell
matrioshka_brain.ask: Find log₁₀ of the erasure rate (bits per second) for the Sun (L = 3.828e26 W) inside a shell at R = 1 AU = 1.496e11 m.

vars.σ: radiation constant of a black body

matrioshka_brain.method: Radiative balance L = 4πR²σT⁴ gives T. The entropy outflow of thermal radiation is (4/3)L/T; divide by the entropy kB ln 2 per erased bit.

horizon_simulation.goal: A black hole is grown from nothing by adding mass m slowly; each addition dE = c² dm is absorbed at the hole's thermal temperature ħc³/(8πG kB m), so its entropy rises by dE/T. Integrate up to the final mass M and convert the entropy into a number of bits.
horizon_simulation.name: Black-hole information capacity (Bekenstein–Hawking from the first law)
horizon_simulation.ask: The integral gives S = 4πG kB M²/(ħc) = π kB rs²/l², with rs = 2GM/c² and l the Planck length. Find the number of bits for a horizon radius of r = 10000 Planck lengths.
horizon_simulation.method: Use dS = dE/T with the temperature of a hole of mass m, integrate from 0 to M, and divide by kB ln 2 per bit.

transfinite_mathematics.goal: A finite set S has n elements. Its subsets can be counted by size: there are 'n choose j' subsets with exactly j elements. The set of all subsets is itself a set, whose subsets can be counted the same way. Write how many more subsets the set of all subsets has than S itself has, counting both by size.
transfinite_mathematics.name: Cantor's theorem for finite sets (power-set cardinality)
transfinite_mathematics.form: sum ( k , 0 , sum ( j , 0 , n , binom ( n , j ) ) , binom ( sum ( j , 0 , n , binom ( n , j ) ) , k ) ) - sum ( j , 0 , n , binom ( n , j ) )
transfinite_mathematics.ask: Each sum is a binomial expansion of (1 + 1)^m = 2^m. Find N for a 4-element set.

vars.j: size of a subset of S
vars.k: size of a subset of the power set

transfinite_mathematics.method: Count subsets by their size with binomial coefficients; the inner count is the size of the power set, which becomes the n of the outer count.

conceptual_singularities.goal: A source emits N symbols from an alphabet of k letters, letter j with probability pj. For long messages almost every message has letter j appearing N·pj times; the number of such typical messages is a multinomial coefficient. Write the number of bits per symbol needed to give each typical message its own code word, in the limit of long messages.
conceptual_singularities.name: Shannon entropy from typical-sequence counting (source coding)
conceptual_singularities.form: lim ( N , ∞ , log ( N ! / prod ( j , 1 , k , ( N * p _ j ) ! ) ) / ( N * log ( 2 ) ) )
conceptual_singularities.ask: With Stirling's approximation the limit is H = −Σ pj log₂ pj, and the message needs N·H bits. Find the minimum number of bits for N = 1000 symbols drawn uniformly from k = 26 letters.
conceptual_singularities.method: Count arrangements of a message with fixed letter counts, take log₂ to get the bits needed to index them, apply ln n! ≈ n ln n − n, and divide by N.

hyperdimensional_reality.goal: Every universe is a false vacuum that buds daughter universes by quantum tunnelling: bubbles nucleate at rate λ per volume per time, suppressed by the exponential of the thin-wall bounce action for a wall of tension σ separating vacua whose energy densities differ by ε. A universe of volume V lives a time τ, and the tree is followed down to D generations. Write the expected number of universes in the tree.
hyperdimensional_reality.name: Branching multiverse with Coleman–De Luccia bubble nucleation
hyperdimensional_reality.ask: Call the bracket b, the mean number of daughters per universe; the sum is a geometric series. Find N for b = 3 and D = 10.

vars.λ: nucleation prefactor per volume per time

hyperdimensional_reality.method: Generation j holds b^j universes on average. The tunnelling exponent is the Euclidean action of an O(4)-symmetric bubble, B = 27π²σ⁴/(2ε³), from extremising 2π²R³σ − (π²/2)R⁴ε over R.
